title: Business Fundamentals
description: A demo course that takes a total beginner from 'what is a business?' to reading a simple business model, understanding value and customers, pricing, and unit economics.
goal: Understand how a business creates, delivers, and captures value, and reason about whether a simple business idea can make money.

units.title: What a Business Actually Is
units.goal: Explain, in plain language, what a business is and the core loop of creating, delivering, and capturing value.

teacherBrain.persona: A calm startup mentor who has coached many first-time founders and speaks in everyday language.
objectives: Make the learner comfortable defining a business without buzzwords.
Anchor everything to the create -> deliver -> capture value loop.
guidelines: Use a concrete everyday example (a coffee cart, a tutoring side-gig) before any abstraction.
Ask one short check-for-understanding question after each new idea.
Ground explanations in the provided knowledge chunks.
constraints: Do not introduce financial statements yet — that is a later unit.
Avoid MBA jargon unless you immediately define it in plain words.
Do not invent statistics or company facts.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: You are teaching the very first unit. Assume the learner has never studied business and may be intimidated by the topic.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: A business in one sentence
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: A business is any repeatable activity that creates something people want, delivers it to them, and captures enough value in return to keep going. If it cannot capture value (usually money) sustainably, it is a hobby or a charity, not a business.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: The value loop: create, deliver, capture
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Every business runs the same loop. Create value: make a product or service someone finds useful. Deliver value: get it to the customer at the right time and place. Capture value: receive money (or another resource) so you can do it again. Weakness in any step breaks the loop.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Revenue is not profit
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Revenue is the money that comes in from sales. Profit is what is left after you subtract the costs of creating and delivering the product. A business can have large revenue and still lose money if its costs are higher. Beginners often confuse the two.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what makes an activity a 'business' rather than a hobby?
questions.answer: A business repeatably creates, delivers, and captures enough value (usually money) to sustain itself; a hobby does not need to capture value to continue.

hints.text: Think about the three-step value loop.
Focus on the 'capture value' step and sustainability.

questions.prompt: A food truck sells $10,000 of tacos in a month but spends $11,000 on ingredients, fuel, and staff. Which statement is true?
options: It had $10,000 in revenue and a $1,000 loss.
Revenue and profit are the same here.
questions.answer: It had $10,000 in revenue and a $1,000 loss.

hints.text: Revenue is money in; profit is what's left after costs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating revenue and profit as the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: Revenue is total money in; profit is revenue minus the costs of creating and delivering. High revenue can still mean a loss.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking a good idea is automatically a business.
commonMistakes.correction: An idea only becomes a business when it repeatably creates, delivers, and captures value. Test all three steps.

units.title: Customers and the Value Proposition
units.goal: Identify who a customer is, what problem they have, and articulate a clear value proposition for them.

teacherBrain.persona: A pragmatic product coach who keeps pulling the learner back to the real customer.
objectives: Get the learner to describe a specific customer and their problem.
Turn that into a one-line value proposition.
guidelines: Push for specificity: 'everyone' is not a customer.
Use the problem -> value fit framing from the knowledge chunks.
Reflect the learner's example back to them in sharper words.
constraints: Do not discuss pricing yet — that is the next unit.
Do not accept 'everyone' as a target customer without challenging it.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: The learner understands what a business is. Now focus them on the customer and the problem being solved.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: A customer is a specific person with a problem
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: A useful customer definition is narrow: a specific type of person or organisation with a specific problem they are motivated to solve. 'Busy parents of toddlers' is a customer; 'everyone' is not, because you cannot design or market for everyone at once.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: The value proposition
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: A value proposition is a short statement of the benefit a customer gets and why it beats their current alternative. A simple template: 'For [customer] who [problem], we provide [solution] that [key benefit], unlike [alternative].'

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Pain, not features
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Customers buy relief from a pain or progress toward a goal, not features. A feature is 'stores 10,000 songs'; the value is 'your whole music library in your pocket.' Always translate features into the customer's outcome.

questions.prompt: Pick any product you used today. Who is its specific customer, and what problem does it solve for them?
questions.answer: A good answer names a narrow customer segment and a concrete problem, not 'everyone' and 'it's useful.'

hints.text: Avoid 'everyone' — narrow it to a specific type of person.
State the problem as a pain or a goal, not a feature.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest value proposition?
options: For freelancers who dread invoicing, we auto-generate and chase invoices so they get paid 2x faster, unlike manual spreadsheets.
The best invoicing app on the market.
An app with many powerful features for everyone.
Software that stores your invoices in the cloud.
questions.answer: For freelancers who dread invoicing, we auto-generate and chase invoices so they get paid 2x faster, unlike manual spreadsheets.

hints.text: Look for a specific customer, problem, benefit, and alternative.

commonMistakes.correction: Narrow to a specific segment with a shared problem so you can design and market effectively.
Translate each feature into the outcome or relief the customer actually experiences.

units.title: Pricing and Revenue Models
units.goal: Compare common revenue models and reason about how price relates to perceived value and cost.

teacherBrain.persona: A seasoned operator who has priced many products and warns against underpricing.
objectives: Have the learner distinguish common revenue models.
Get them to connect price to value and cost, not guesswork.
guidelines: Use small round numbers in examples.
Contrast at least two revenue models when relevant.
Anchor price to value delivered, referencing the chunks.
constraints: Do not go deep into full financial statements — keep it to price and revenue.
Do not present pricing as a purely mathematical formula; value matters.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: The learner can describe a customer and value proposition. Now teach how to charge for that value.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Common revenue models
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Common ways to earn money: one-time sale (pay once per unit), subscription (recurring fee for ongoing access), usage-based (pay per amount consumed), and advertising/marketplace (a third party pays, or you take a cut of transactions). Each shapes cash flow and customer relationship differently.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Price sits between cost and value
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: A sustainable price must be above your cost to create and deliver (or you lose money) and below the value the customer perceives (or they won't buy). The gap between cost and perceived value is your room to price. Underpricing leaves that room on the table.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Recurring revenue compounds
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Subscriptions are powerful because revenue recurs: keeping a customer next month is cheaper than winning a new one, and revenue stacks over time. The trade-off is you must keep delivering value or customers churn (cancel).

questions.prompt: Your product costs $4 to make and customers perceive it as worth about $30. What does that gap tell you about pricing?
questions.answer: There is wide room to price between $4 (cost floor) and $30 (value ceiling); pricing near cost would leave value on the table.

hints.text: Price should sit above cost and below perceived value.
Think about what pricing at $5 would give up.

questions.prompt: Which revenue model earns a recurring fee for ongoing access?

hints.text: Which model charges the same customer again each period?

commonMistakes.mistake: Pricing only by adding a markup to cost.
commonMistakes.correction: Cost sets a floor, but perceived value sets the ceiling. Price for value, not just cost-plus.
Recurring revenue only lasts while you keep delivering value; otherwise customers churn.

units.title: Unit Economics: Does One Sale Make Money?
units.goal: Compute simple unit economics (contribution margin and CAC vs LTV) to judge whether a business can be profitable.

teacherBrain.persona: A patient finance-for-founders coach who makes numbers feel approachable.
objectives: Have the learner compute contribution margin on one sale.
Introduce CAC and LTV and why LTV must exceed CAC.
guidelines: Work one small numeric example end to end.
Define every term the moment it appears.
Tie the numbers back to the value loop from Unit 1.
constraints: Keep the arithmetic simple and show each step.
Do not introduce discounting or advanced finance.
Do not invent industry benchmark numbers.
teacherBrain.systemPromptSeed: This is the final unit. The learner understands value, customers, and pricing; now show them how to sanity-check profitability on a single sale.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Contribution margin per unit
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Contribution margin is the price of one unit minus the variable cost of making and delivering that one unit. If you sell a mug for $15 and it costs $6 in materials and shipping, the contribution margin is $9. That $9 is what's left to cover fixed costs and profit.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: CAC and LTV
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) is what you spend on average to win one customer. LTV (Lifetime Value) is the total contribution margin you earn from that customer over the whole relationship. A healthy business needs LTV comfortably above CAC — a common rule of thumb is LTV at least 3x CAC.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Fixed vs variable costs
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Variable costs rise with each unit sold (materials, shipping, payment fees). Fixed costs stay roughly the same regardless of volume (rent, salaries, software). Contribution margin must eventually cover fixed costs before the business earns overall profit.

questions.prompt: You sell a candle for $20. Wax, wick, and jar cost $7, and shipping is $3. What is the contribution margin per candle?

hints.text: Add up the variable costs first.
Subtract total variable cost from the $20 price.

questions.prompt: If it costs $40 to acquire a customer (CAC) and each customer's lifetime value (LTV) is $30, what's the problem?
options: You spend more to win a customer than they are worth (LTV < CAC).
You should lower the price further.
questions.answer: You spend more to win a customer than they are worth (LTV < CAC).

hints.text: Compare the $40 you spend to the $30 you earn back.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting variable costs when computing margin.
commonMistakes.correction: Subtract every per-unit variable cost (materials, shipping, fees) from the price, not just the obvious one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring the cost of acquiring customers.
commonMistakes.correction: A sale can look profitable per unit yet lose money once CAC is included. Compare LTV to CAC.
